from_quote: the houſe of repreſentatives is to be choſen by the people once in two years
rationale: The paragraph says the House of Representatives is chosen by the people once in two years, as Article I, Section 2, Clause 1 provides.
to_quote: chosen every second Year by the People of the several States

from_quote: one man is to repreſent 30,000 ſouls
rationale: The paragraph gives the ratio of one representative to 30,000, the figure in Article I, Section 2, Clause 3.
to_quote: one for every thirty Thousand

from_quote: men of ripe age, who have been, at leaſt, ſeven years citizens of the United States, and, at the time of election, reſidents of the reſpective ſtate
rationale: The paragraph states the age, seven years' citizenship and residence required of a representative, the qualifications of Article I, Section 2, Clause 2.
to_quote: been seven Years a Citizen of the United States

from_quote: another houſe, conſiſting of men ſtill more ſelect, poſſeſſing ſuperior qualifications of reſidence and age
rationale: The paragraph says the senate is made up of men with higher qualifications of residence and age than the House, which refers to the qualifications for Senator in Article I, Section 3, Clause 3.
to_quote: been nine Years a Citizen of the United States

from_quote: the bill muſt be ſubmitted to the objections of the preſident
rationale: The paragraph says a bill that has passed both houses is submitted to the objections of the president, the presentment procedure of Article I, Section 7, Clause 2.
to_quote: be presented to the President of the United States

from_quote: He is elected by perſons choſen for that ſpecial purpoſe
rationale: The paragraph says the president is elected by persons chosen for that special purpose, which describes the electors of Article II, Section 1, Clause 2.
to_quote: a Number of Electors

from_quote: a compenſation, which cannot be diminiſhed or
rationale: The paragraph says the president's compensation cannot be diminished or increased during his continuance in office, as Article II, Section 1, Clause 7 provides. Part of the word "increased" is lost in the scan; the quoted words come before it.
to_quote: a Compensation, which shall neither be encreased nor diminished

from_quote: The term of his commiſſion is limited to four years
rationale: The paragraph says the president's term is limited to four years, as Article II, Section 1, Clause 1 provides.
to_quote: during the Term of four Years

from_quote: of holding elections for ſenators and repreſentatives, ſhall be preſcribed in each ſtate
rationale: The paragraph, headed "Art. 1, sect. 4," reproduces the first clause of Article I, Section 4 (the printed commas differ slightly from the clause).
to_quote: of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State

from_quote: Let congreſs, even officiouſly, exert every power given by this clauſe, the repreſentatives muſt ſtill be choſen by the people, and the ſenate by the ſtate legiſlatures
rationale: The paragraph discusses "this clause," the Article I, Section 4 clause quoted in the preceding paragraph, and its effect on how representatives and senators are chosen.
to_quote: except as to the Places of chusing Senators

from_quote: his ſalary can be neither augmented nor curtailed, during his commiſſion
rationale: The paragraph says the president's salary can be neither augmented nor curtailed during his commission, as Article II, Section 1, Clause 7 provides.
to_quote: a Compensation, which shall neither be encreased nor diminished

from_quote: No member can be appointed to an office, created, or of which the profits
rationale: The paragraph restates the first part of Article I, Section 6, Clause 2 (no member to be appointed to an office created, or whose profits were increased, during his term). Some words of the sentence are lost in the scan; the quoted words come before the gap.
to_quote: be appointed to any civil Office under the Authority of the United States, which shall have been created, or the Emoluments whereof shall have been encreased during such time

from_quote: by the privilege of nominating perſons to office, the preſident will find the congreſs
rationale: The paragraph takes up the president's "privilege of nominating persons to office," the nomination power of Article II, Section 2, Clause 2.
to_quote: he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint

from_quote: againſt conſtituting the ſenate a council to the preſident
rationale: The paragraph defends "constituting the senate a council to the president," which names the Senate's share in treaties and appointments under Article II, Section 2, Clause 2.
to_quote: by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate

from_quote: The ſenate are to try impeachments.
rationale: The paragraph says the senate is to try impeachments, as Article I, Section 3, Clause 6 provides.
to_quote: The Senate shall have the sole Power to try all Impeachments

from_quote: By their advice only, may the preſident make treaties, appoint ambaſſadors, miniſters, conſuls, judges of the ſupreme court, and officers, not otherwiſe provided for in the conſtitution
rationale: The paragraph lists the treaties and appointments the president may make only by the Senate's advice, in words that follow Article II, Section 2, Clause 2.
to_quote: Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States, whose Appointments are not herein otherwise provided for

from_quote: elected for only four years
rationale: The paragraph says the president is elected for four years, the term in Article II, Section 1, Clause 1.
to_quote: during the Term of four Years

from_quote: thoſe electors give their ſuffrages on the ſame day, in thirteen different aſſemblies, in thirteen different ſtates
rationale: The paragraph says the electors vote in different assemblies in thirteen different states, which describes the meeting of the electors in their respective states under Article II, Section 1, Clause 3.
to_quote: The Electors shall meet in their respective States

from_quote: thoſe electors give their ſuffrages on the ſame day
rationale: The paragraph says the electors give their votes on the same day, as Article II, Section 1, Clause 4 provides.
to_quote: which Day shall be the same throughout the United States

from_quote: the ſweeping clauſe
rationale: The paragraph names "the sweeping clause" and introduces it as "the clause" quoted in the next paragraph, which is the last clause of Article I, Section 8.
to_quote: To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers

from_quote: the power of raiſing fleets and armies, without any ſtint or limitation, in time of peace
rationale: The paragraph names the power of raising armies in time of peace among the objections to the powers of congress, which is the army clause of Article I, Section 8, Clause 12.
to_quote: To raise and support Armies

from_quote: the power of raiſing fleets and armies, without any ſtint or limitation, in time of peace
rationale: The paragraph names the power of raising fleets (as well as armies) in time of peace among the objections to the powers of congress, which is the navy clause of Article I, Section 8, Clause 13.
to_quote: To provide and maintain a Navy

from_quote: for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers veſted by this conſtitution
rationale: The paragraph, headed "Art. 1, sect. ..., par. the last," quotes the last clause of Article I, Section 8. A word of the printed clause is lost in the scan, and the commas differ slightly in the full quotation; the quoted words are identical.
to_quote: for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution

from_quote: this ſweeping clauſe will afford pretext, for freeing congreſs from all conſtitutional reſtraints
rationale: The paragraph refers to "this sweeping clause," the clause quoted two paragraphs earlier, which is the last clause of Article I, Section 8.
to_quote: To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers

from_quote: No act of congreſs ſhall be valid, unleſs it have relation to the foregoing powers, and be neceſſary and proper for carrying them into execution
rationale: The paragraph restates the "necessary and proper" clause as meaning that no act of congress is valid unless it relates to the foregoing powers and is "necessary and proper for carrying them into execution."
to_quote: which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers

from_quote: Without this general clauſe, it were eaſy to ſuppoſe caſes, wherein a particular clauſe might be incompetent to its own purpoſe
rationale: The paragraph refers to "this general clause" in the discussion of the clause quoted earlier, the last clause of Article I, Section 8.
to_quote: To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers

from_quote: it is provided in the conſtitution, that each ſtate ſhall officer, and train its own militia
rationale: The paragraph says the constitution provides that each state shall officer and train its own militia, which describes the reservation in Article I, Section 8, Clause 16.
to_quote: reserving to the States respectively, the Appointment of the Officers, and the Authority of training the Militia

from_quote: The judiciary power is to be veſted in one ſupreme court
rationale: The paragraph restates Article III, Section 1: the judiciary power vested in one supreme court, with inferior courts that congress may appoint.
to_quote: vested in one supreme Court

from_quote: To all caſe, in which may be concerned an ambaſſador, any other public miniſter, or a conſul.
rationale: The paragraph lists, as the first head of the supreme court's original jurisdiction, cases concerning an ambassador, other public minister or consul, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 2 does.
to_quote: In all Cases affecting Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls

from_quote: To all caſes whatever, in which a ſtate may be a party.
rationale: The paragraph lists, as the second head of the supreme court's original jurisdiction, all cases in which a state is a party, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 2 does.
to_quote: and those in which a State shall be Party

from_quote: Caſes between two or more ſtates. 3. Caſes between a ſtate, and its own citizens. 4. Caſes between a ſtate, and the citizens of another ſtate. 5. Caſes between a ſtate, and a foreign ſtate.
rationale: The paragraph divides the cases in which a state is a party into heads (between states, between a state and citizens of another state, between a state and a foreign state), which follow the list of controversies in Article III, Section 2, Clause 1.
to_quote: between two or more States

from_quote: in law and equity, ariſing under this conſtitution
rationale: The paragraph, listing the appellate jurisdiction of the supreme court, reproduces the words "in law and equity, arising under this constitution" from Article III, Section 2, Clause 1.
to_quote: in Law and Equity, arising under this Constitution

from_quote: To all caſes of admiralty or maritime juriſdiction.
rationale: The paragraph lists cases of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 does.
to_quote: all Cases of admiralty and maritime Jurisdiction

from_quote: To all caſes, in which the United States ſhall be a party.
rationale: The paragraph lists cases in which the United States is a party, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 does.
to_quote: Controversies to which the United States shall be a Party

from_quote: To all caſes between citizens of different ſtates.
rationale: The paragraph lists cases between citizens of different states, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 does.
to_quote: between Citizens of different States

from_quote: To all caſes between citizens of the ſame ſtate, claiming lands under the grants of different ſtates.
rationale: The paragraph lists cases between citizens of the same state claiming lands under grants of different states, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 does.
to_quote: between Citizens of the same State claiming Lands under Grants of different States

from_quote: To all caſes between citizens of a ſtate, and foreign ſtates, or their citizens or ſubjects.
rationale: The paragraph lists cases between a state's citizens and foreign states or their citizens or subjects, as Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 does.
to_quote: between a State, or the Citizens thereof, and foreign States, Citizens or Subjects

from_quote: congreſs is to make ſuch regulations and exceptions, as upon mature deliberation, it ſhall think proper
rationale: The paragraph says congress is to make "regulations and exceptions" for appeals, which refers to the clause of Article III, Section 2, Clause 2 giving appellate jurisdiction "with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make."
to_quote: with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make

from_quote: the judges, holding their commiſſions during good behaviour
rationale: The paragraph speaks of "the judges, holding their commissions during good behaviour," which refers to the tenure of judges in Article III, Section 1.
to_quote: shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour

from_quote: The propoſed plan expreſsly adopts it, for the deciſion of all criminal accuſations, except impeachment
rationale: The paragraph says the plan "expressly adopts" trial by jury for all criminal accusations except impeachment, which describes Article III, Section 2, Clause 3.
to_quote: The Trial of all Crimes, except in Cases of Impeachment, shall be by Jury

from_quote: By recogniſing the jury trial in criminal caſes, the conſtitution effectually provides, that it ſhall prevail
rationale: The paragraph speaks of the constitution's recognition of jury trial in criminal cases, which is Article III, Section 2, Clause 3.
to_quote: The Trial of all Crimes, except in Cases of Impeachment, shall be by Jury

from_quote: When we were told, that the celebrated Mr. Wilſon had advanced this doctrine in effect
rationale: The paragraph says Mr. Wilson had advanced "this doctrine" (that a federal power must be conferred by the compact, so that a bill of rights is not needed) "in effect." Wilson's address of October 6, 1787, which predates this pamphlet, makes that argument in its second paragraph; the speech is not named, so the link rests on the speaker's name and the doctrine.
to_quote: every thing which is not given, is reſerved

from_quote: It provides, that no man ſhall ſuffer by expoſt facto laws, or bills of attainder. It declares, that gold and ſilver only ſhall be a tender for ſpecie debts; and that no law ſhall impair the obligation of a contract.
rationale: Following a sentence on "the restraints laid on the state legislatures," the paragraph lists the prohibitions on ex post facto laws and bills of attainder, on tender other than gold and silver, and on laws impairing contracts, which are in Article I, Section 10, Clause 1.
to_quote: No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation

from_quote: a renunciation of the right to emit bills of credit
rationale: The paragraph says the convention saw that a renunciation of the right to emit bills of credit was needed, which refers to the ban on state bills of credit in Article I, Section 10, Clause 1.
to_quote: emit Bills of Credit

from_quote: if I underſtand the man who ſtyles himſelf a Centinel, he inſinuates, that, if theſe ſtates will perſiſt in remaining under one head, they muſt ſoon fall under the dominion of a deſpot
rationale: The paragraph names a writer who styles himself Centinel and answers his argument that the states cannot remain under one government without falling to a despot. Centinel I (October 5, 1787), the only Centinel essay in the library before this pamphlet (January 1, 1788) that argues this, says so in its twenty-first paragraph; the essay is worked out from the subject and date.

from_quote: treaty, alliance, or confederation
rationale: The paragraph, listing what an individual state will lose, reproduces the words "treaty, alliance, or confederation" of Article I, Section 10, Clause 1 and goes on with the other prohibitions of that clause.
to_quote: Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation

from_quote: She ſhall not, without conſent of congreſs, lay any duty on imports or exports, except what may be neceſſary for executing her inſpection laws.
rationale: The paragraph restates the limit on state duties on imports and exports, with the exception for inspection laws, in the words of Article I, Section 10, Clause 2.
to_quote: No State shall, without the Consent of the Congress, lay any Imposts or Duties on Imports or Exports

from_quote: unleſs actually invaded, or in ſuch imminent danger
rationale: The paragraph restates the limits on state duties of tonnage, troops, compacts and war in the words of Article I, Section 10, Clause 3, ending with the exception for actual invasion.
to_quote: unless actually invaded, or in such imminent Danger
